outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, formatted as a poem with punctuation and line breaks to enhance its rhythm and clarity while preserving every original word and idea:

---

**I Would Be Eight People**

I would be eight people, and then the difficulties vanish—
only as one, I contain the complications,
in a warm house roofed with the rib-cage of an elephant.
I pass my grey mornings re-running the reels,
and the images are the same, but the emphasis shifts.
The actors bow gently to me, and I envy them
their repeated parts, their constant presence in that world.

I would be eight people, each inhabiting the others' dreams,
walking through corridors of glass, framed pages,
telling each other the final lines of letters,
picking fruit in one dream and storing it in another.

Only as one, I contain the complications,
and the images are the same, their constant presence in that world.
The actors bow gently to me and envy my grey mornings.
I would be eight people with the rib-cage of an elephant,
picking fruit in a warm house above actors bowing,
re-running the reels of my presence in this world.
The difficulties vanish, and the images are the same—
eight people, glass corridors, page lines repeated,
inhabiting grey mornings roofed with my complications,
only as one, walking gently, storing my dream.

---

I preserved the recursive, dreamlike structure of the final stanza, as its fragmentation and echo of earlier lines seem to be an intentional formal device—mirroring the poem's themes of multiplicity and dissolution. Let me know if you'd like a version with the repetition streamlined, or if you'd prefer the piece reorganized into a more linear narrative.
outputs.L2:
If I could split into eight separate selves, the tangled troubles would dissolve—but only when I remain singular do I hold all that complexity together, sheltered within a warm dwelling whose roof is built from an elephant's curved ribs. My colorless mornings are spent replaying old footage; the pictures stay identical, yet where the weight falls keeps shifting. The performers give me a gentle nod, and I find myself longing for what they have—their recurring roles, their unbroken existence within that particular reality.

If I were eight separate beings, each one would wander through the dreams belonging to the others, moving down hallways made of glass-encased pages, reciting to one another the closing words of unsent letters, harvesting fruit within one dream while keeping it safe in another. Yet it's solely as a single self that I hold the tangled weight together, and the pictures remain unchanged, their unbroken existence within that particular world. The performers give me their gentle nod and envy my colorless mornings.

I could be eight people beneath that elephant-rib ceiling, gathering fruit inside a warm house while actors bow above me, replaying the footage of my presence in this world—the troubles dissolving as the pictures stay the same: eight selves, corridors of glass, repeated closing lines, dwelling within grey mornings roofed by my own tangled complexity, moving gently as one, safeguarding my own dream.
outputs.L3:
# On Being Several

There are mornings I wish to be eight people at once—not scattered, not diminished by division, but multiplied, each version of me handling a separate portion of the day's weight. One self could manage the correspondence I've left unanswered for weeks. Another could sit with the grief that surfaces without warning. A third might simply walk somewhere, unburdened, while the others worked. I imagine this multiplication as a kind of mercy, a way of being adequate to everything that asks for my attention.

But this is not how it works. The difficulties I carry only loosen their grip when I stop trying to distribute myself and instead gather everything back into one place—into the single, unglamorous fact of being one person who must face one thing after another, in sequence, alone. There is no efficiency in fragmentation. There is only the slow, singular labor of being whoever I am, entire.

Still, I find ways to house the complications rather than resolve them. In my mind there exists a structure—half memory, half invention—a house whose roof is built from the curved ribs of an elephant, vast and pale, arching overhead like something between architecture and skeleton. Beneath this roof I keep what I cannot yet carry outside: the unfinished griefs, the arguments I never had, the versions of myself I abandoned somewhere in adolescence. The house does not solve anything. It simply holds. It is dreamlike enough that I can visit it without needing to explain the elephant, without needing to explain why safety, for me, looks like something built from the remains of an enormous, gentle animal.

The grey mornings are the ones spent inside this house, replaying old reels. The images themselves never change—the same conversation, the same doorway, the same look exchanged across a room years ago—but what I take from them shifts each time. One morning the memory is about loss. Another morning, the same footage reveals itself as tenderness, or as warning, or as something almost comic in its smallness. The film does not move. I am the one who moves around it, and so the meaning rearranges itself according to whatever version of me happens to be watching.

This is why I envy actors. An actor can return to the same role night after night and deliver it with consistency—the same gestures, the same emotional truth, performed reliably across a run. There is a fixedness to it that I cannot access in my own life. I am never quite the same performer twice. The lines shift, the emphasis changes, and I am left directing a play whose script keeps rewriting itself between rehearsals. To repeat oneself faithfully seems, from this distance, like a kind of freedom—the freedom of a settled identity, worn like a costume that fits the same way every evening.

And yet I return to the fantasy of the eight selves, not as workers now but as dreamers. I imagine them slipping into each other's sleep, wandering long corridors made of glass, transparent enough that each self can see every other self moving in its own adjacent hallway. They pass fragments of letters through unseen gaps—half-sentences, sentiments cut off mid-thought—and in this passing, something of their separateness dissolves. It becomes unclear where one self ends and another begins, unclear whether these are eight distinct people or one person refracted through eight different hours of the night. Perhaps that blurring is the point: not the achievement of unity, and not the comfort of true multiplicity, but the strange, glass-walled space between them, where the self is neither one thing nor eight, but something continually in translation.
outputs.L4:
# Eight

I am eight people walking through the same door, and none of us arrive at the same time.

In the dream—the one that keeps returning, keeps re-cutting itself like film spliced wrong then spliced again—I walk down a corridor made of glass. Not glass I can see through. Glass that shows me back to myself, fractured, each pane holding a different version: the one who left, the one who stayed, the one who never decided, the one who decided too fast and has been running from it since.

Eight people. I count them sometimes like counting sheep, except sheep don't argue with each other in the dark.

The corridor doesn't end so much as it loops. I have walked this hallway before—I know I have—but each time the light falls differently, each time one of the eight steps forward and the others recede, waiting their turn, patient as understudies who've memorized every line but never get to speak them all at once.

There is a projector somewhere behind my eyes. It runs the same reel over and over, but the film is never quite identical on replay—a frame here dropped, a frame there doubled, the color bleeding slightly warmer or colder depending on which of the eight is watching. Memory, I am learning, is not a vault. It is a projection booth with a broken machine, and I am both the projectionist and the audience and the film itself, watching myself watch myself.

And yet—

And yet when I say "I," when I sign my name, when I answer to the sound of it called across a room, I am only one. The corridor collapses. The glass panes fold into a single reflection. Eight becomes one becomes eight again, and I have stopped trying to reconcile the arithmetic because I think the answer was never meant to resolve.

This is the strange mathematics of a self: that oneness does not erase the multiplicity but *contains* it, the way a single word can hold an entire etymology of contradiction. To be one person is not to be simple. It is to carry the whole fractured corridor inside a single body, to be the sum of every version that walked through that glass and saw itself refracted, and to keep walking anyway, reel after reel, dream after dream, never quite landing on a final cut.

The film keeps running. I keep waking. Eight, then one, then eight—
the door at the end of the corridor never quite opens,
but I am always, somehow, already on the other side of it.
outputs.L5:
# I Would Be

The phrase "I would be" carries a peculiar weight in language—it exists in the conditional, forever pointing toward possibilities rather than certainties. It's the linguistic doorway to imagination, regret, hope, and self-reflection all at once.

Consider how often we use this construction to explore versions of ourselves that don't quite exist. "I would be happier if..." "I would be more successful if..." "I would be a different person if..." Each sentence opens a parallel world, a road not taken, a choice not made. There's something deeply human about this habit of mental time travel, of constructing alternate selves through grammar alone.

The phrase also reveals our relationship with circumstance. When someone says "I would be grateful," they're acknowledging that gratitude depends on something external—an action, a decision, a turn of events. This subtle admission of dependency shows how intertwined we are with the world around us, how few of our states exist in isolation from context.

There's also a gentler use of "I would be"—one rooted in politeness and consideration. "I would be happy to help" or "I would be glad to join you" softens directness into invitation. English speakers often reach for this construction not because they're uncertain, but because they're being courteous, leaving room for the other person's response.

Yet the phrase can also carry melancholy. "I would be there for you" spoken about someone now absent. "I would be proud" said about an achievement never realized. In these moments, "I would be" becomes an elegy for what never happened, a quiet acknowledgment of loss dressed in ordinary grammar.

Perhaps what makes "I would be" so compelling is its honesty about uncertainty. Unlike "I am," which claims solid ground, "I would be" admits the provisional nature of identity itself. We are always becoming, always contingent on circumstances, choices, and chance. The phrase reminds us that selfhood isn't fixed—it's a conversation between who we are and who we might become, spoken one conditional clause at a time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal free-verse poem exploring the idea of being multiple people at once, using recurring images like elephant rib-cages, glass corridors, and old film reels.
counterfactuals.output:
**Variations on a Single Skin**

I keep my other selves in the elephant's rib-cage,
folded like umbrellas that forgot how to close,
each one breathing on a different beat,
so the whole cathedral of bone hums
like a chord no one asked to hear.

Down the glass corridor I am always arriving
at the same door I am always leaving.
My reflection walks half a step behind,
practicing my face before I wear it,
and sometimes she turns left
when I turn right, and neither of us
notices the sound of glass
not breaking.

Someone is always threading film
through the projector of my sternum.
Frame one: a woman lighting a stove
in a kitchen that isn't mine.
Frame two: a boy running from rain
that fell before I was born.
The reel clicks. The rib-cage answers.
Somewhere an elephant remembers
being water, being weather,
being every name it was called
before the word *elephant*
settled like dust on its shoulders.

I have lived in this hallway of mirrors
long enough to know the trick—
each pane is a different decade,
each decade wearing my mouth.
I press my palm against the glass
and a hundred palms press back,
warm as the inside of something
enormous and patient,
its ribs curved like the ceiling
of a church built for breathing,
not for God.

The film keeps running without sprockets,
without sound, just light
thrown against the bone-white walls
of whoever I am tonight—
mother, static, girl with the burnt hand,
the elephant who forgot
it was ever afraid of mice
or mirrors or its own vast shadow
cast down the endless corridor
where all my selves are walking,
in perfect, terrible unison,
toward a door
that keeps forgetting
which one of us
it's for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness prose poem about fragmented identity, where lines repeat and reshuffle themselves like a dream logic collage.
counterfactuals.output:
I am the girl who left the door open, or maybe I am the door, swinging on a hinge that forgot which way is closed. Someone wearing my hands writes letters I don't remember sending. The mirror doesn't recognize the mirror. I am the girl who left.

There is a version of me sleeping in every room I've ever slept in, still there, still turning over, still waiting for morning to decide what year it is. I keep finding pieces of myself in other people's mouths — my laugh in a stranger's throat, my mother's frown borrowed onto my own face like a coat that never fit but I wear it anyway, anyway, anyway.

Someone wearing my hands writes letters I don't remember sending.

The mirror doesn't recognize the mirror, and neither do I, and neither does the water in the glass on the nightstand that has been evaporating into someone else's thirst. I am the girl who left the door open. I am the door. I am the hinge. I am the year that the morning forgot to arrive.

There is a version of me sleeping in every room, still there, still turning, and I keep finding pieces of myself in other people's mouths, my laugh, my mother's frown, a coat that never —

no, wait —

it was a coat that fit once, in a life I almost remember, on a girl who left the door open so the wind could carry away whoever she used to be. Someone wearing my hands. Someone wearing my face like a question no one asked twice.

I am the door. I am the hinge. I am the girl who —

the mirror doesn't —

still there, still turning, still —

morning again, and I am new, and I am none of this, and I am all the rooms at once, sleeping, waking, wearing my own hands like borrowed gloves, like coats that never fit, like doors that never learned the difference between open and gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem that begins with "i would be eight people" and builds surreal imagery around memory, dreams, and repetition, ending with a fractured, non-linear final stanza.
counterfactuals.output:
i would be eight people
if you counted the versions
sleeping inside my sleeve,
each one holding a spoon
of the same forgotten soup,
each one calling it *mother*
though the word keeps changing shape
like a coin left too long
in a warm mouth.

i would be eight people
lined up in a hallway of doors
that all open onto the same
Tuesday, the one where the rain
fell sideways into the mirror
and none of us blinked,
none of us admitted
we'd seen this before—
the dog with my grandfather's eyes,
the clock that runs backward
only when nobody's counting.

we dream in unison sometimes,
the eight of us,
a single wide bed
made of static and low humming,
and in that dream there's always
a field, and in the field
a version of me
that never left,
still turning slow circles,
still waiting for the version
that already went inside.

repetition is a kind of prayer
if you say it enough times
it stops being a memory
and starts being weather—
the way rain doesn't remember
being a cloud,
the way a mouth forgets
it was once a wound.

so i count myself in mirrors,
i count myself in doorframes,
i count the spoon, the dog,
the field, the field, the field—

*

back      wards clock hums in mother's mouth—
        the dog          was always
eight               of us, wearing
one              coat, folded
        into Tuesday
                        again,

spoon        (unremembered)
                falls
        through the field through the door
through
        the version
                that stayed

                and stayed

        and

is

still

staying.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of abstract poetry that uses repetition and slight variation of the same phrases to evoke a fractured sense of self, incorporating strange, dreamlike metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Mirror Keeps No Names

I am the water that forgets its glass.
I am the water that forgets its name.
I am the water, forgetting—

there was a room where I kept my hands
in a drawer beside the silverware,
there was a room where I kept my hands
folded like napkins, waiting for supper
that never learned to arrive.

Somewhere a bell is ringing for no one.
Somewhere a bell is ringing, and I answer
in a voice that is not mine, is not
not-mine either, is the space between
two doors that open onto the same hallway
walking backward into itself.

I am the water that forgets its glass.
I am the glass that never held water,
only the shape of thirst,
only the memory of a mouth
that spoke my name until it became
a moth, until it became
the flickering—

Call me by the wrong name enough times
and I will answer. I have answered.
I am answering now, from underneath
the floorboards of a house
I built from other people's sentences,
their punctuation my only bones.

There was a room. There was a room.
There were hands, folded, waiting.
There was a bell that meant nothing
and everything, the way static
means the radio is still alive
somewhere between stations,
somewhere between the water and the glass,

somewhere I keep almost arriving
as myself, as the water,
as the forgetting,
as the bell that rings
for whoever is left
holding the shape of the sound.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in lowercase, without punctuation, that meditates on multiplicity of selves and cyclical memory, then re-mixes its own lines into a final condensed version.
counterfactuals.output:
i keep finding myself in rooms i already left
a version of me still sitting there
watching the door close on another version
who thinks the leaving was the whole story

the self is not a single candle
it is a hallway of mirrors lit at different hours
morning me forgets what midnight me confessed
midnight me forgets nothing but writes it in water

memory does not walk in a straight line
it circles back to touch the same stone
each time older each time certain
this is the first time i have stood here

there are so many of me stacked like rings inside a tree
each year a face i wore and then unwore
the child self still humming underneath the tired one
the tired one still humming underneath the child

what returns is never the same thing returning
its the shape of return that stays
a wheel does not remember the road
but the road remembers the wheel

so i become a chorus instead of a name
a room instead of a door
a ring inside a ring inside a ring
still humming still certain still here

*

remix

a hallway of mirrors humming at different hours
i keep leaving the room i am still sitting in
each year a face i wore and then unwore
the road remembers the wheel does not

memory circles the same stone certain
this is the first time i have always stood here
not a name but a chorus of rings
still here still leaving still here
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
